Note the separate "Non-profits with no paid staff" category is narrower than the open-source category; apply under open source, which is the cleaner claim. ADVERSARIAL VET 2026-08-03: All six tests pass on eligibility, so I cannot reject it on the claim — but it survives as a weak candidate, hence fit 2 rather than the submitted framing. (1) The quoted sentence "Open-source projects, including projects with a small paid team." appears verbatim on the page, in the list introduced by "The following types of organizations are generally eligible for a free Zulip Cloud Standard plan." ArtaQuest qualifies on that line alone (AGPL-3.0, public repo) and arguably on two more: "Research in an academic setting" and "Non-profits with no paid staff." (2) No US-only clause, no 501(c)(3) requirement, no equivalency determination, no geography lock — I hunted specifically and found the opposite: "Zulip sponsors free plans for over 1000 worthy organizations" and a separate line offering extra help to orgs abroad ("Discounts are available for organizations based in the developing world"). A Canadian registered charity is not excluded anywhere on the page. (3) Organisation-level, not an individual fellowship. (4) It is a genuine donation of service, not a discount: the page keeps the two tracks explicitly separate — sponsorship is a "free" Standard plan, while "Education organizations are eligible for education pricing" and the developing-world line are the discount track. Only the free-plan track is being claimed here, which is the right one; the discount tracks would fail the hard filter. No affiliate scheme, no ad-sales desk.

grants.title: .ORG Impact Awards
grants.funder: Public Interest Registry, the non-profit operator of the .ORG top-level domain, Reston…
grants.amount_display: Cash, paid as unrestricted donation funds to the winning organisation ("use the award funds however they see fit"). Finalists…
grants.summary: Free to enter, organisation-only, explicitly worldwide, self-application, and the money is real and unrestricted-in-practice ($10,000 per category winner, $40,000 for .ORG of the Year, $2,500 just for being a finalist). ArtaQuest holds artaquest.org, which is the sole eligibility hook. The story travels well in this format — a charity that makes research checkable by strangers, in 133 languages, at no cost — and finalist money alone would seed a member challenge pool. EVIDENCE: "The .ORG Impact Awards are open to organizations using a .ORG domain." and "The program is open to organizations and individuals around the world, except where prohibited by law." (both https://pir.org/for-orgs/entering-the-oias/)
grants.red_flags: Eligibility hinges on 'organizations using a .ORG domain' — artaquest.org currently 301-redirects to artaquest.com, so we are a .ORG holder but arguably not a .ORG *user*; before entering, either stand up a real page on artaquest.org or get PIR to confirm in writing that a redirecting .ORG counts. Keep the .org renewed regardless. Cycle CLOSED until roughly April 2027. Fit is generic social impact, not research — judged against food banks and health charities, a reproducibility platform is a hard sell, and the award is a PR programme for the .ORG brand, so expect to supply a marketing-grade story. Money is framed as a 'donation award', so check it can be received by a Canadian charity. ADVERSARIAL VET 2026-08-03: Both quoted sentences appear verbatim on the target page, and the eligibility claim survives adversarial testing: this is a genuinely worldwide, free, self-nomination award with no US 501(c)(3) clause, no equivalency determination, and no Canada exclusion — the only geographic bars are sanctions jurisdictions (Iran, DPRK, Sudan, Syria, Crimea). Non-US organisations demonstrably receive the money: the 2025 .ORG of the Year was DRC-based (Fonds pour les Femmes Congolaises), with winners/finalists from India, Kenya, Uganda, Cameroon, Rwanda, Senegal, Indonesia and Liberia. It is real cash to an organisation ("Winning organizations have the flexibility to use the award funds however they see fit"), not a discount, affiliate scheme or ad-sales desk, and six of the seven categories are org-level (only Rising Star is the individual one). So it is not a reject. But three material conditions must be named. (1) TIMING: the proposal's "deadline: none stated" is wrong and misleading — PIR's page states flatly "2026 submissions are now closed." Submissions closed 27 May 2026; finalists are announced 11 August 2026 and the ceremony is 6 October 2026. Nothing is actionable for roughly eight months.

grants.title: Grand Challenges (open calls / Requests for Proposals)
grants.summary: Grand Challenges is the Gates Foundation's OPEN-proposal entry point (most other Gates funding is invitation-only); nonprofits/researchers/orgs worldwide may submit to a specific challenge RFP. BUT current 2026 RFPs are all GLOBAL HEALTH / Global-South (AI-in-health, malaria modelling, neglected tropical diseases, health data-science). ArtaQuest fits only IF a future call covers education / AI-for-learning.
grants.red_flags: Current calls are health-sector + Global-South-focused; no general-education call open now. Treat as a watch-list — monitor for an education/learning/AI-in-education Grand Challenge.

grants.title: Education Cannot Wait — Acceleration Facility (global public goods, thematic Calls for Proposals)
grants.funder: Education Cannot Wait (ECW), the UN global fund for education in emergencies, hosted/administered by UNICEF
grants.country: Global / United States (ECW is hosted by UNICEF; secretariat in New York).
grants.summary: Legally registered national or international organisations, UN agencies/entities, international NGOs, civil society organisations, academic institutions, foundations, and organisations of persons with disabilities — that have the capacity to deliver education-in-emergencies and protracted-crisis (EiEPC) programming or global public goods for that sector. Applicants typically must be registered on relevant UN partner portals and hold a HACT low/medium risk rating. Consortium-based applications are strongly encouraged with a lead organisation holding the grant agreement. Access is limited to invited partners or organisations responding to a specific thematic RFP.
grants.red_flags: STRONG MISFIT for ArtaQuest. (1) Thematic scope is strictly education in EMERGENCIES and protracted crises (refugees, conflict, displacement) — not general open educational resources or a global online learning platform; ArtaQuest's mission does not fit the EiEPC mandate. (2) AF funds "global public goods" (products, tools, coordination bodies, research, data systems) for the EiE sector — NOT scholarships/bursaries or financial aid regranted to individual learners, which is one of ArtaQuest's two funding goals. (3) Invitation/RFP-only: no unsolicited applications accepted; no path for a small early-stage charity to apply outside a matching thematic call. (4) Practical eligibility gate: applicants generally must be UN partner-portal-registered with a HACT risk rating and the scale/track record to absorb a multi-million-dollar grant — far beyond a small early-stage org. (5) Recipients to date are large UN agencies and established global coalitions, not small national charities.

grants.title: The Daily Grant (micro-grant program)
grants.summary: Compassion-driven individuals, informal groups, and registered nonprofits ANYWHERE (Canada eligible). Designed for EARLY-STAGE / grassroots seed projects (<$10k total budget) — marginal for an established platform; ArtaQuest could seed only a tiny new community initiative.
grants.red_flags: Micro-seed only (~$500, <$10k project budget) and aimed at early-stage/grassroots — low fit for an established org. Keep as a long-shot/seed option.
